title: Hospital Price Compare
tagline: Real THB prices for the same procedure at Bumrungrad, Bangkok Hospital, Samitivej and public hospitals
problem: Self-pay patients in Bangkok cannot see what an appendectomy, MRI or birth package will cost until the bill arrives, and the same procedure can cost several times more at one private hospital than another. A Commerce Ministry review found 295 of 353 private hospitals marking prices well above cost, and Thai media regularly report bills like 30,000 baht for a diarrhoea admission. Hospital websites show promotional packages only, so expats on high-deductible plans and Thais without corporate cover guess blind.
solution: A bilingual price index that combines hospitals' published package pages, the DIT-mandated price disclosures, and crowdsourced itemised receipts that users upload (OCR strips names before storage). Each procedure page shows a median, range and 'what was actually billed' versus the advertised package, split by private tier (Bumrungrad/Bangkok Hospital/Samitivej), mid-tier chains and public or university hospitals with private wings. Users can request a written estimate from up to three hospitals in one form, and get alerted when a package promo drops. Unlike HDmall, which sells checkup packages, it covers inpatient and surgical prices and shows real bills, not only list prices.
target_audience: Self-pay expats and retirees in Bangkok; Thais with only SSO or UC cover choosing private care; insured expats with deductibles; medical tourists
business_model: Freemium + paid estimate requests + hospital lead fees
pricing: Free search; ฿199 per multi-hospital estimate request; Pro ฿149/month for alerts and bill history; hospitals pay ฿300–800 per qualified lead (est.)
score_justification: L4 OCR+LLM normalise receipts; E3 seeding prices takes weeks; A4 recurring overcharge news and forum asks; P3 SEO + Pantip/expat FB groups; M5 crowdsourced real bills compound; W3 users pay for estimates, hospitals for leads
platform_distribution: Google SEO (EN+TH procedure-cost queries); Pantip Sukhaphap room; expat Facebook groups; LINE OA for estimate requests
tam_source: bottom-up: ~2M self-pay or high-deductible private-hospital episodes/yr × ฿600 blended lead + estimate revenue (est.)
competitors: HDmall; Bookimed; hospital package pages (Bumrungrad, Samitivej); DIT price disclosure
competitor_gap: HDmall and Bookimed sell packages and show list prices only; nobody publishes what itemised inpatient bills actually came to
demand_evidence: Bangkok Post reported 295 of 353 private hospitals marking up well above cost, and the DIT has pushed hospitals to publish prices online, showing both demand and a policy tailwind.
unique_data_capture: Itemised real-bill database by hospital, procedure, length of stay and payer type; it compounds because each upload sharpens the medians and exposes package-vs-actual gaps no hospital will publish
commoditization_risk: Medium: HDmall could extend to inpatient pricing, but hospitals resist publishing real bills and a general AI assistant has no receipt data
regulatory_notes: Health data is sensitive personal data under PDPA s.26: explicit consent, a DPO-level policy, Thai-hosted or contractually protected storage and breach notification within 72h. Defamation (Criminal Code s.326) risk when naming hospitals; publish aggregates and verified receipts only, no clinical advice.
founder_feasibility: Solo-founder feasible. A foreigner can run this as an offshore SaaS/info service (e.g. a Singapore or US entity) billing Thai users online; a Thai company with 51% Thai ownership or a BOI digital-service promotion is needed only once it hires staff, signs Thai B2B contracts at scale or takes commissions as a local service business under the Foreign Business Act List 3. Lead fees from hospitals push it toward a Thai entity.
mvp_features: Procedure price pages with ranges; anonymised receipt upload with OCR; multi-hospital estimate request; promo alerts via LINE; tier filter (private/public/university)
tech_stack: Next.js + Supabase + OCR + LLM API (Claude/GPT) for line-item normalisation + LINE Messaging API
review_notes: Cold start: needs a few thousand real receipts before medians are trustworthy; a Thai co-founder is needed for hospital lead deals.

title: Hospital Bill Check
tagline: Upload a Thai hospital bill; get flagged drug markups, duplicate charges and a dispute letter in Thai
problem: Thai private hospital bills bundle drugs, supplies and 'service fees' into long itemised lists that patients sign off at discharge under time pressure. Consumer groups have documented drug prices up to about 200% above pharmacy or public-hospital prices, and the Commerce Ministry has found hidden charges in specific cases. Most patients never learn that they can ask for an itemised bill, call the DIT 1569 hotline or complain to the Department of Health Service Support, so overcharges stand.
solution: A LINE and web tool where users photograph a bill or estimate; OCR plus an LLM maps each line to a reference price drawn from the DIT drug price list, public-hospital prices and the platform's own crowdsourced bills. It flags outsized drug markups, duplicate or unrendered items and charges that should be covered by the patient's insurance or UCEP emergency rules. It then drafts a polite Thai or English query letter to the hospital billing office and, if needed, a complaint to 1569 or the Consumer Protection Board. This is a Thailand-specific adaptation of the US bill-audit idea, built on Thai price references.
target_audience: Thai families paying private hospital bills out of pocket; expats with deductibles or no cover; HR teams reviewing employee claims
pricing: Free red-flag scan; ฿290 full audit report with letter; 15% of any refund above ฿5,000; B2B ฿15,000/month for HR/broker bulk checks

tam_source: bottom-up: 1M disputed-worthy private bills/yr × ฿600 blended revenue (est.)
competitors: DIT 1569 hotline; Consumer Protection Board; Foundation for Consumers; insurance brokers' claim desks
competitor_gap: Government channels act only after a complaint and need the patient to know what is wrong; no tool reads the bill line by line against reference prices
demand_evidence: Matichon reported consumer-group findings of drug prices nearly 200% above pharmacy prices and bills of ฿430,000; The Nation runs explainers on where to complain about hospital overpricing.
unique_data_capture: Line-item price observations by hospital and drug SKU plus dispute outcomes (refund or not), which become a negotiation playbook and a reference-price set no one else has
commoditization_risk: Medium: a general AI assistant can read a bill but lacks Thai reference prices and dispute outcome data

Avoid giving legal advice beyond template letters (Lawyers Act); no clinical judgement on whether treatment was needed.

title: Expat Claim Fighter
tagline: Bilingual help to file, track and appeal denied health insurance claims in Thailand
problem: Expats and retirees in Thailand buy local or international health policies, then discover at claim time that the insurer has pulled records from every Thai hospital they ever visited and denied the claim as pre-existing. ASEAN NOW threads are full of members describing denials, partial payments only after escalating to the Insurance Ombudsman, and premiums jumping after a claim. Policy wording is often Thai-first, deadlines are short, and few expats know the OIC complaint route.
solution: A claim-support service that ingests the policy schedule and wording (Thai or English), the hospital records and the denial letter, then explains in plain English which clause the insurer is relying on and whether the 'pre-existing' look-back actually applies. It assembles a timeline from the user's records, drafts an appeal letter and, if needed, an OIC (Office of Insurance Commission) complaint in Thai, and tracks deadlines. Paid tiers add a Thai-speaking case handler who calls the insurer. Unlike brokers, who are paid by insurers, it works only for the policyholder.
target_audience: Retirees on O-A/O-X visas with mandatory insurance; digital nomads and DTV holders; Thai spouses handling claims for foreign partners
pricing: ฿990 claim review; ฿2,900 appeal pack with Thai OIC filing; 10% of recovered amount above ฿20,000
score_justification: L4 LLM parses policy and denial; E4 doc workflow + human handler; A4 many ASEAN NOW denial threads; P3 expat forums and FB groups; M4 denial-reason and outcome database by insurer; W4 claims are often ฿100k+ so expats pay
platform_distribution: ASEAN NOW forum; expat Facebook groups (Hua Hin, Pattaya, Chiang Mai); Google SEO for 'claim denied Thailand'
tam_source: bottom-up: ~50,000 disputed expat claims/yr × ฿3,000 avg revenue (est.)
competitors: Insurance brokers (Pacific Prime, AA Insurance Brokers); Insurance Ombudsman/OIC; ASEAN NOW forum advice
competitor_gap: Brokers are insurer-paid and focus on selling renewals; OIC requires a Thai-language complaint the user must prepare alone
demand_evidence: ASEAN NOW threads on claim denials and pre-existing exclusions describe insurers pulling prior hospital records and members escalating to the ombudsman to get partial payment.
unique_data_capture: Structured denial reasons, clauses cited, insurer, outcome and time-to-pay; it compounds into an insurer reliability score and winning appeal templates
commoditization_risk: Low: needs Thai-language filing, case handling and outcome data a general assistant lacks
regulatory_notes: Health data is sensitive personal data under PDPA s.26: explicit consent, a DPO-level policy, Thai-hosted or contractually protected storage and breach notification within 72h. Acting for a fee in insurance disputes must avoid acting as an unlicensed broker (OIC) or giving legal services; position as document prep and advocacy, partner with a Thai lawyer for litigation.
founder_feasibility: Solo-founder feasible. A foreigner can run this as an offshore SaaS/info service (e.g. a Singapore or US entity) billing Thai users online; a Thai company with 51% Thai ownership or a BOI digital-service promotion is needed only once it hires staff, signs Thai B2B contracts at scale or takes commissions as a local service business under the Foreign Business Act List 3. A Thai-speaking case handler (contractor) is needed from day one.
payment_rails: Cards via Stripe/Omise; PromptPay QR; Wise transfers
mvp_features: Policy and denial upload with clause explainer; record timeline builder; appeal letter generator; OIC complaint draft in Thai; deadline tracker
tech_stack: Next.js + Supabase + OCR + LLM API (Claude/GPT) + Thai translation review
review_notes: This adapts the generic claim-coach idea to Thai expat insurance; the risk is low win rates on genuine pre-existing exclusions.

title: Prescription Price Finder
tagline: Compare what your hospital charges for a drug with nearby pharmacy prices before you fill it
problem: Patients discharged from Thai private hospitals routinely pay hospital pharmacy prices for chronic drugs that independent pharmacies sell for a fraction, and one petitioner described nearly ฿100,000 in three months of cholesterol and antacid drugs. The government has tried QR codes for about 3,000 drugs to let buyers compare pharmacy and hospital prices, but there is still no consumer app that shows live prices by pharmacy. Expats on ASEAN NOW repeatedly ask what a given medicine should cost without insurance.
solution: A LINE-first app where users snap a prescription or hospital drug list, and it matches each drug by generic name and strength to prices from chain pharmacies (Boots, Watsons, Fascino, Pure), partner independents and the DIT reference list. It shows the cheapest nearby option on Google Maps, legal generic equivalents with the same active ingredient and whether the drug is prescription-only, and it lets partner pharmacies reserve the order for pick-up. Pharmacies pay to list prices and for reservations. It gives price information only, not dosing advice, and directs questions to the pharmacist.
target_audience: Chronic-condition patients (diabetes, hypertension, cholesterol); caregivers buying for elderly parents; expats paying out of pocket
pricing: Free for patients; Plus ฿59/month for refill reminders and family lists; pharmacies ฿990/month listing + ฿20 per reservation
score_justification: L4 OCR + drug-name matching; E3 price feeds need partnerships; A4 petitions and expat price threads; P4 LINE + Google Maps; M4 SKU-level price history across pharmacies; W3 pharmacies pay for footfall, patients rarely pay
platform_distribution: LINE OA; Google Maps pharmacy pages; TikTok price-comparison clips; Facebook chronic-disease groups
tam_source: bottom-up: 25,000 pharmacies × 5% paying ฿12,000/yr + reservation fees, plus 200k Plus subscribers (est.)
competitors: DIT drug price QR initiative; Boots/Watsons apps; HDmall pharmacy; MorDee medicine delivery
competitor_gap: Chain apps show only their own prices and the DIT list is static; no cross-pharmacy price comparison against the hospital's charge
demand_evidence: The Nation reported the DIT plan to QR-code ~3,000 drugs so buyers can compare pharmacy and hospital prices; ASEAN NOW threads ask what medicines cost without insurance.
unique_data_capture: Pharmacy-level SKU price observations over time and hospital-vs-pharmacy spreads; compounds with every scan and pharmacy feed
commoditization_risk: Medium: chains or LINE MAN could add comparison, but each chain only shows its own prices
regulatory_notes: Health data is sensitive personal data under PDPA s.26: explicit consent, a DPO-level policy, Thai-hosted or contractually protected storage and breach notification within 72h. Drug Act: the app must not sell or advertise prescription-only drugs to consumers or give dispensing advice; pharmacies must hold FDA licences.
founder_feasibility: A marketplace taking commissions on Thai services is a List 3 'other service' under the Foreign Business Act, so a foreign founder needs a Thai-majority company, a Foreign Business Licence or BOI promotion (digital platform category) to operate locally; an offshore entity with a Thai co-founder handling partner contracts is the usual MVP path.
mvp_features: Prescription photo to generic-name list; pharmacy price compare map; generic equivalent display; reserve-for-pickup; refill reminders via LINE
tech_stack: LINE LIFF + Next.js + Postgres + OCR + LLM API (Claude/GPT) + Google Maps API
review_notes: Pharmacy price feeds are the hard part; independents may not want transparent pricing.

title: Therapist Match Thailand
tagline: Find a licensed Thai or English-speaking psychologist with real prices, specialties and wait times
problem: Thailand has about 1.3 psychiatrists per 100,000 people, over ten times below the global average, and six provinces have no psychologist at state hospitals at all. Thais who want help hit stigma and waitlists, while expats need a therapist who speaks English (or their language) and understands visa or relationship stress. Prices vary from free hotlines to ฿3,000+ per hour at private clinics, and it is hard to tell a licensed clinical psychologist from an unlicensed 'life coach'.
solution: A bilingual directory and matching quiz that lists licensed psychiatrists, clinical psychologists and counsellors across private clinics, hospital departments and platforms such as Ooca and iSTRONG, with price per session, language, modality (online/in person), specialties and next available slot. Licence status is checked against the Medical Council and the Thai psychology licensing register. Users answer a short non-diagnostic preference quiz (language, budget, issue area, gender preference) and get three matches with booking links. Revenue comes from provider listings and booking fees, not from delivering care, so it does not practise telemedicine itself. This is a Thai market adaptation of the generic therapist-match directory.
target_audience: Thai office workers 22–40; university students; expats and their partners; HR teams referring staff outside EAP
pricing: Free for users; providers ฿1,500/month premium listing; ฿100 booking fee per first session; corporate referral desk ฿20,000/month

competitors: Ooca; iSTRONG; MorDee mental-health doctors; Alljit (free chat); hospital psychiatry departments
competitor_gap: Ooca and iSTRONG list only their own clinicians; nobody compares across clinics with prices, languages and licence checks
demand_evidence: The Nation (Jan 2026, citing Thai Health 2025) reported 1.3 psychiatrists per 100,000 and that 89% of Thais did not access mental-health services in the past year.
unique_data_capture: Provider availability, real session prices and post-session satisfaction by provider; moderate moat as providers can list elsewhere

title: Dental Price Tracker
tagline: Implant, braces and veneer prices and patient-reported outcomes for Bangkok dental clinics
problem: Dental implant quotes in Bangkok range from about ฿24,000 to over ฿100,000 per tooth depending on brand, abutment and crown, and aggregator listings conflict even with themselves. Patients cannot compare like for like because clinics quote implant-only, crown-only or all-in prices, and few disclose the implant brand or the dentist's specialty. Medical-tourism brokers show 5-star ratings with no follow-up on failures a year later.
solution: A price and outcome tracker for dental procedures that normalises quotes into an all-in price (fixture brand, abutment, crown, bone graft, follow-ups) from user-uploaded quotes and clinic submissions. Each clinic page shows price ranges by procedure, dentist licence verified against the Dental Council, specialty training and 6-, 12- and 24-month follow-up surveys sent automatically via LINE or email. A quote-checker lets users paste a clinic quote and see whether it is high, typical or low for that brand. Unlike Bookimed or WhatClinic, it tracks outcomes after the visit and works for local Thais as well as tourists.
target_audience: Thais 35–65 needing implants or crowns; expats and retirees; dental tourists from Australia, Europe and the Gulf

title: Beauty Clinic Verify
tagline: Check a Thai beauty clinic's licence, the injector's credentials and complication reports before booking
problem: Thailand's aesthetic boom has produced a wave of illegal clinics: police raided a foreign-run laser clinic on Koh Phangan after burns, an unqualified person was arrested at a Srinagarind clinic, and a Public Health Ministry official said in 2026 that they see daily reports of harm from facial injections. The official checks exist (hosp.hss.moph.go.th for clinic licences, tmc.or.th for doctors) but they are in Thai, separate, and a licensed clinic can still use an unlicensed injector. Buyers on TikTok and Instagram rarely check.
solution: A bilingual verification layer that, given a clinic name, LINE ID or Instagram handle, pulls the DHSS licence record, licence type (whether it can legally do surgery or only minor procedures), listed doctors and their Medical Council status. It adds a public complication and complaint log sourced from news reports and user submissions with photo evidence, and a 'what to ask before you book' checklist. A browser and LINE share card shows a green/amber/red status that users can send to friends. Verified clinics pay for a badge and procedure price list; revenue never depends on hiding complaints.

competitor_gap: Official checks are Thai-only, disconnected and do not show complaint history or whether the injector matches the licence
demand_evidence: Pattaya Mail and Thai PBS report officials urging the public to check clinic licences online, and Khaosod and Thai PBS World covered 2025 raids on illegal clinics.

title: Checkup Package Decoder
tagline: See exactly which tests each hospital checkup package includes, which you need, and the cheapest match
problem: Thai hospitals sell annual checkup packages from about ฿3,000 to over ฿60,000, and Bumrungrad's 2026 campaign brochures alone list dozens of packages with promotional columns that are hard to read. Packages differ in tests (CEA, CA-125, low-dose CT, echocardiogram) that most buyers cannot interpret, so people overbuy cancer markers or miss age-appropriate screens. Employers and families buying for parents compare brochures by hand.
solution: A decoder that parses package brochures and listing pages into a standard test list, then builds a side-by-side table: price per package, tests included, tests missing and price per comparable test. A short profile (age, sex, family history) maps to public screening guidance from the Thai Department of Health and international bodies, showing which tests are commonly recommended and which are optional, without diagnosing. Users see the cheapest package that covers their chosen list across private, mid-tier and public hospitals and can buy through affiliate links. It differs from HDmall by being neutral across sellers and explaining tests.

pricing: Free for consumers; 5–10% affiliate commission on packages; HR comparison report ฿4,900 per company

title: SSO Hospital Picker
tagline: Choose the best Social Security hospital for your needs before the annual switch window closes
problem: Thailand's Social Security Office lets Section 33 and 39 insured workers change their registered hospital once a year (16 Dec 2025 to 31 Mar 2026 for the 2026 cycle), and the choice decides where they get almost all non-emergency care for a year. Workers pick on location or rumour because there is no structured comparison of wait times, specialist access, referral friction, dental and maternity handling across the roughly 270 SSO hospitals (est.). Pantip threads asking 'which SSO hospital is good' recur every year.
solution: A Thai-first LINE OA and web tool that lists every SSO-contracted hospital with crowdsourced wait times, ease of specialist referral, chronic-drug availability, satisfaction ratings and distance from home and work. Users enter their needs (pregnancy, diabetes, child under 6, commute) and get a ranked shortlist and a reminder before the switch window opens, then step-by-step instructions to switch on SSO Plus or the sso.go.th site. After each visit, a two-question LINE survey updates the scores. Hospitals cannot pay for ranking; revenue comes from employer HR dashboards and optional add-ons such as private OPD top-up insurance referrals.
target_audience: ~12M SSO Section 33 workers (est.); Section 39 self-insured; factory and retail HR teams; migrant workers with SSO cover
business_model: Freemium B2C + employer HR subscription + insurance referral
pricing: Free for workers; employers ฿3,000/month HR dashboard for staff hospital choice; top-up insurance referral fees
score_justification: L3 AI summarises reviews; E4 LINE OA + hospital list in weeks; A4 annual switch season drives searches and Pantip posts; P5 LINE OA reaches workers directly; M4 visit-level wait-time data compounds; W2 workers won't pay, employer sales slow
platform_distribution: LINE OA; TikTok during Dec–Mar switch season; Facebook factory-worker groups; Pantip
tam_source: bottom-up: 10,000 employers × ฿12,000/yr HR plan (est.)
competitors: SSO Plus app and LINE @ssothai; Google Maps reviews; Pantip threads
competitor_gap: The SSO's own channels handle the switch but give no quality comparison; Google reviews mix private-patient experiences
demand_evidence: FlowAccount and Thansettakij publish yearly how-to guides for the SSO hospital switch, showing a recurring seasonal search need.

title: Surgery Quote Compare
tagline: Send one case file, get itemised surgery quotes from vetted Thai hospitals and surgeons in 72 hours
problem: Foreign and Thai self-pay patients needing a knee replacement, hernia repair or spinal surgery email hospitals one by one and receive non-comparable package quotes that exclude implants, extra nights or complications. Medical-tourism brokers earn hidden commissions of 15–30% (est.) and steer patients to paying partners. Patients cannot easily check the surgeon's credentials, case volume or what happens if the stay runs long.

Quotes come back in the same format: surgeon, implant brand, nights included, per-extra-night price, complication cover and what is excluded. The platform checks surgeon licences on the Medical Council site and shows a fixed, disclosed referral fee. Post-surgery follow-ups feed an outcome score. This differs from the existing SEA medical-tourism concept by being a neutral RFQ marketplace with disclosed fees and itemised comparisons, open to Thai self-pay patients too.

title: Care Home Check

title: Parents Daily Check-in

problem: Millions of Thai adults in Bangkok have ageing parents living alone or with a spouse in the provinces, and about 65% of falls among older people happen at home. title: Pet Friendly Condo Verify

title: Pet Move Planner
tagline: Step-by-step DLD permits, vet paperwork and airline quotes for moving a pet into or out of Thailand
problem: Expats moving to or leaving Thailand with a pet face conflicting advice on DLD import permits, rabies titres for some origin countries, health certificate timing and possible quarantine, and getting it wrong means a pet held at Suvarnabhumi. Door-to-door relocation agents charge ฿50,000+ and airline cargo fees run ฿15,000–60,000. Guides from different sites disagree on fees and titre rules.
solution: A planner where owners enter origin, destination, species, breed and travel date; it generates a dated checklist from official DLD rules and destination rules (e.g. Australia, EU, UK, US) with deadlines for microchip, vaccines, titre tests and health certificates. It drafts the DLD permit request email, lists airlines accepting the breed and crate size on that route with prices, and offers a vetted Thai vet for export paperwork. Owners can buy a DIY plan or request quotes from relocation agents, who pay per lead. It also works for Thais emigrating with pets.
target_audience: Expats relocating to or from Bangkok, Phuket and Chiang Mai; Thai families emigrating; digital nomads with cats

tam_source: bottom-up: 15,000 pet moves/yr in/out of Thailand × ฿5,000 blended revenue (est.)
competitors: PetRelocation; Jetpets; WorldCare Pet Transport; DIY via DLD guidance
competitor_gap: Agents are expensive and opaque; DIY guides conflict and don't produce a dated, route-specific plan
demand_evidence: Multiple 2026 guides (PetRelocation, Superagent, ZooVet Travel) give conflicting rules on titres and permits, and Superagent reports door-to-door packages of ฿50,000+.
unique_data_capture: Route-by-route outcomes (delays, holds, actual airline fees) from completed moves; modest but useful moat

A foreigner can run this as an offshore SaaS/info service (e.g. a Singapore or US entity) billing Thai users online; a Thai company with 51% Thai ownership or a BOI digital-service promotion is needed only once it hires staff, signs Thai B2B contracts at scale or takes commissions as a local service business under the Foreign Business Act List 3. title: Pet Insurance Claim Score
tagline: Compare Thai pet insurance by real claim payouts, not brochures, for cats and dogs
problem: Thai pet insurance is a sub-฿200M market, about 0.2% of pet spending, partly because owners don't trust policies they can't compare. Plans from Muang Thai, Viriyah and FWD cap vet fees around ฿40,000 a year with exclusions by breed and age, and price is often 'on request'. Owners only find out what is covered when a claim is rejected.
solution: A comparison and claim-outcome site: owners enter species, breed and age to see eligible plans, premiums, annual limits and exclusions decoded into plain Thai and English. Its differentiator is a claims ledger: owners upload claim outcomes (paid, partial, denied, days to pay) alongside the vet bill, so each insurer gets a payout score by condition. It earns broker-partner commission on policies sold through a licensed Thai broker and sells anonymised claims insights to insurers designing products. Pet owners can also check whether a planned surgery is likely to be covered.

competitor_gap: Giraffy and CheckDi compare premiums and limits; none show actual claim payout behaviour
demand_evidence: Thairath reports the market is below ฿200M (0.2% of pet spending) while cat ownership grew 32.1% in 2025, signalling under-penetration and growth.

title: International School Compare

title: Thai School Scorecard

problem: Thousands of foreigners study Thai on ED visas paying about ฿30,000–80,000 a year, but in 2025 immigration tightened rules and revoked nearly 10,000 student visas, and schools must now track attendance and students may be tested in Thai at extension. Students cannot tell compliant, good schools from visa mills, and many finish a year still unable to hear tones. Apps like Ling and glot.it teach vocabulary but don't prepare learners for real conversations or an immigration officer's spot test.

First, a scorecard of Thai language schools: Ministry of Education accreditation, ED visa compliance record, class sizes, teaching method, fees and verified student progress surveys (CEFR-style self and tested levels). Second, an AI speaking coach with pitch-contour tone feedback, role plays for market, taxi, landlord and immigration-interview scenarios, and weekly progress reports schools can use as attendance-plus-learning evidence. Schools pay to integrate the coach for their students; individual learners subscribe.

title: IELTS Speaking Mock TH
tagline: AI speaking examiner tuned to Thai learners' errors, for IELTS and international-programme interviews
problem: Thailand ranked 116th of 123 countries in the 2025 EF English Proficiency Index, falling into the 'very low' band, yet Thai students applying to international programmes, scholarships and jobs abroad need IELTS band 6–7 speaking scores. It tracks band estimates over time and recommends drills; a paid tier adds a human examiner review once a month. title: TCAS Chance Planner
tagline: Enter your TGAT, TPAT and A-Level scores; see each programme's weighted score and admission odds
problem: Every year about 200,000 Thai Grade 12 students (est.) navigate TCAS rounds, where each faculty weights TGAT, TPAT and A-Level scores differently and round 3 lets them rank up to 10 choices. Students compute weighted scores by hand from dozens of announcement PDFs, and past minimum scores are scattered, so many waste ranked choices on unreachable programmes or miss safer ones. Tutoring schools charge for counselling that is mostly arithmetic.
solution: A planner that ingests every programme's published weighting formula and historical minimum and maximum scores, then calculates the student's weighted score for each programme instantly. It estimates admission odds bands (reach, match, safe) from past cut-offs and applicant numbers, and suggests a 10-choice ranking strategy that balances preferences and risk. It sends LINE reminders for each round's dates and document deadlines, and parents get a summary view. Unlike mytcas.com (the official application system) and Dek-D (news and community), it does the per-programme maths and strategy.
target_audience: Thai Grade 11–12 students; parents; dek ซิ่ว retakers; school guidance counsellors; tutoring schools
pricing: Free calculator; Premium ฿199 per admission season (odds + strategy + reminders); school licence ฿9,900/yr
score_justification: L4 LLM parses announcement PDFs into formulas; E4 calculator MVP in weeks; A5 every Thai student goes through TCAS; P4 TikTok/LINE student culture; M3 formula database copyable, odds data better; W3 students pay small amounts, parents more

tam_source: bottom-up: 200,000 candidates × 15% × ฿199 + 1,000 schools × ฿9,900 (est.)
competitors: mytcas.com; Dek-D; TruePlookpanya; tutoring-school counselling services
competitor_gap: Official and media sites publish rules and news but don't compute personalised weighted scores and odds across all programmes
demand_evidence: Thai PBS reported confusion when round 3 didn't publish minimum scores and faculties counted points differently; MHESI subsidises TGAT/TPAT fees for TCAS 2569 applicants.
unique_data_capture: Self-reported student scores and actual admission outcomes, improving odds models each year beyond official cut-offs
commoditization_risk: Medium: Dek-D or a general AI assistant could add calculators, but outcome-calibrated odds need user data
regulatory_notes: PDPA: students are often minors (under 20 needs parental consent for some processing); no guarantees of admission in marketing.

A foreigner can run this as an offshore SaaS/info service (e.g. a Singapore or US entity) billing Thai users online; a Thai company with 51% Thai ownership or a BOI digital-service promotion is needed only once it hires staff, signs Thai B2B contracts at scale or takes commissions as a local service business under the Foreign Business Act List 3. title: Verified Tutor Results
tagline: Find Thai tutors by verified student score gains, with recorded trial lessons and fair-price ranges
problem: Thai parents spend heavily on private tutoring, a multi-billion-baht market, yet choose tutors from Facebook posts and claims like 'students got into Chula' that can't be checked. Hourly rates range from ฿300 to ฿2,000+ with no link to results, and directories such as BestKru list thousands of tutors with self-written profiles. Expat parents also look for Thai-language or IGCSE tutors and have no quality signal.
solution: A tutoring marketplace where tutors earn a 'verified results' badge by linking student score reports (school grades, TGAT/A-Level, IGCSE, IELTS) before and after a tutoring period, uploaded by the parent with consent. Every tutor offers a short recorded trial lesson that the platform scores for clarity and engagement with AI plus parent ratings. Parents filter by subject, exam, language (Thai/English) and price, and see the fair rate range for that subject and level. Bookings and payments go through the platform with PromptPay and session notes are posted to LINE.

pricing: Free to browse; 15% commission on lessons (typical ฿400–1,200/hour); tutors ฿290/month Pro for promoted profile
score_justification: L3 AI scores trial lessons and matches; E3 two-sided marketplace and verification flow; A4 large tutoring spend; P4 LINE and parent FB groups; M4 verified score-gain data; W4 parents already pay tutors weekly

tam_source: https://journal.unisza.edu.my/jonus/index.php/jonus/article/download/184/120 (tutoring ~฿8.2B in 2015) as market base

competitor_gap: Directories rely on self-written profiles; none verify score improvements or provide comparable trial lessons
